title: Focus day 22-09-01 - Semantic Release Versioning and GitHub Runners
content:
Attendees:

Semantic Release Versioning

We offer support with a variety of workflows, but we lack templatized support for semantic versioning. Release versioning is often something that falls behind when implementing CI/CD, yet it is absolutely critical to be able to identify exact versions running in production; making sure the versions are idempotent and traceable.

While it’s partly the solution architects' and teams' responsibility areas, it is evident that some teams would benefit from guidance and assistance with patterns on how to address proper versioning.

Semantic versioning, as a concept, may seem pretty straight-forward, but when adding automation, changelogs and various pipelines the complexity rises. Below are some common questions:

  • Should we use a fully automated semantic versioning approach, or semi automated?

    • When, and in what stage, do we bump major?

  • What are the pros and cons of existing solutions?

    • https://github.com/semantic-release/semantic-release

    • https://github.com/marketplace/actions/git-semantic-version

    • …

Adding to this we need to find and bind a proper solution for the actual git tags. Note: The version as specified in e.g. package.json does not necessarily constitute the actual release version. And what is a proper way to implement a trigger? Many solutions use the commit messages, but is this always the correct approach? If you perform 50 commits on a README.md file, should you specify “patch” for each of these commits? “50 patches?”

This topic, release versioning, has gained even more importance during our assistance with the Sofa migrations, as both Sofa, and Storage Two, enforce a version when creating a release candidate, but how does the person who triggers the workflow know how to set the appropriate version? For example, there may be 5 pull-requests merged for a release; one with a major breaking change, one with a minor change, and three with patch updates only. How is this tracked?

We also need to take into consideration that some teams have abandoned npm semver, as it did not fit their release model.

One idea that I’m currently thinking of is:

  • Use pull-request titles to denote the change (major, minor, patch)

    • Each single commit has no relevance; it is the totality (like a squashed commit) that counts

    • When the pull-request is closed, and merged, (not abandoned), create a tag with major, minor, and patch

      • To avoid concurrency issues we add a unique build number to the tag; e.g., v1.5.2.44

Then, when creating a release candidate, the correct (and latest tag) already exists, so the input field is only optional (if one would like to override the latest tag). If the latest tag is v1.5.2.44 then it’s possible to give the tag name “v1.5.2.44-RC1” (release candidate 1) when performing a release candidate deployment to CTE/PPE.

As can be discerned there are different ways of tackling this problem, and seldon one solution fits all teams. But we need to have a steering framework on this topic:

  • How to best support our customers (the teams)

    • How to guide them during different release scenarios

  • Scaffolded workflows that can perform some of this work

    • Currently, there are limited logical GitHub actions on the marked place that tackle this issue.

      • Workflows such as “create a tag” is not very interesting - the complexity goes far beyond this

  • Potentially we could create an action ourselves that:

    • Creates a tag based on:

      • input

        • pull-request title

        • commit message

        • labels

        • etc

      • Correctly updates the major, minor, and patch version

      • Partial code for this already exists

Suggestion on work breakdown:

: Architecture, design, and patterns - find potential best practices that suites the general IPEX planner/product - use cases. & : Investigation of current solutions, both on the marked, and in IPEX. Prototyping, PoCs, etc. Investigation of potential pitfalls and shortcomings of certain solutions. Investigating and finding teams and products that have a successful release and tag versioning model - what else could be improved for these teams? Also checking teams that have some semantic versioning model implemented, but that may not work satisfactory. Plus, finding teams that lack a good versioning strategy model, or teams that do not have appropriate tagging.
